l: Minyan heroes, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: The heroes travel through the city in armor, prepare and launch Argo, sacrifice to Apollo, and sail from Pagasae. They choose Jason as leader, assign rowing places, listen to Orpheus’s song, and pass along the coast before reaching Lemnos.

l: Argonauts, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: The Argonauts are the heroes who undertake the voyage from Iolcos to the land of Aeetes in search of the Golden Fleece. They launch Argo, sail past the shores of Magnesia and Thrace, and arrive at Lemnos.

l: Heracles, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Heracles refuses the leadership offered to him and urges the heroes to choose Jason, the man who brought them together. He shares the middle bench with Ancaeus, helps drag and launch Argo, and kills one of the sacrificial steers with his club.

l: Argus, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Argus son of Arestor comes from the city despite Pelias’s wishes and joins the heroes. He wears a bull hide and directs the heroes to gird the ship with a tightly twisted rope.

l: Tiphys, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Tiphys is entrusted with the helm of Argo. He boards the ship to coordinate its launching, later skillfully guides it from the harbour, and wakes the heroes so they can prepare to depart.

l: Ancaeus, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Ancaeus shares the middle bench with Heracles. He helps kill one of the sacrificial steers by striking its neck with a bronze axe.

l: Idmon, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Idmon watches the sacrificial flame and interprets Apollo’s will. He says that the heroes are destined to return with the fleece, but that countless trials await them and he himself will die somewhere on the mainland of Asia.

l: Orpheus, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Orpheus stops the quarrel between Idas and Idmon by playing his lyre and singing of the origins of the earth, heaven, sea, gods, and other beings. During the voyage he plays and sings as the heroes row.

l: Zeus, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Zeus is invoked in the customary libations after Orpheus’s song. Idas also claims that no venture will fail even if a god opposes Jason, and Idmon recalls the destruction of the sons of Aloeus by Zeus’s divine opposition through Leto’s son.

l: Apollo, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Apollo is asked to guide Argo and the heroes safely to the land of Aeetes and back to Hellas. Jason sacrifices steers to him, and the heroes later pour libations in honor of Zeus after Orpheus’s song.

l: Athena, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Athena is said to have brought the divine beam from the oak of Dodona and fitted it into the middle of Argo’s stem. Jason also takes courage from Athena’s promises.

l: Aeetes, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Aeetes is the ruler whose land the heroes intend to reach. The people of the city say that the heroes might destroy his palace with fire if he did not willingly yield the fleece.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Argo is prepared, dragged over rollers, and launched into the sea at Pagasae. The heroes fit it with oars, mast, sails, stores, and a divine beam, then sail it along the coast to Lemnos.

l: golden fleece, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: The Golden Fleece is the object of the expedition to the land of Aeetes. Idmon prophesies that the heroes will return with it.

l: Apollo of the Dawn, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Apollo Embasius is honored with an altar on the shore before the ship departs. Jason prays to him to guide the ship and grant favorable winds, fulfilling the oracle that prompted the voyage.

l: the oracle of Apollo, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: The oracle of Apollo promised Jason that Apollo would show him the paths of the sea if he began the venture with sacrifice. Jason relies on this oracle when organizing the departure.

l: Idmon’s prophecy, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Idmon’s prophecy declares that the heroes will return with the fleece but will face countless trials on the outward and homeward journeys. It also declares that Idmon will die somewhere on the mainland of Asia.

l: Argonauts’ voyage, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: The Argonautic expedition begins when Jason and the heroes leave Pagasae to seek the fleece in Aeetes’ land. The expedition includes the preparation and launch of Argo, the sacrifice to Apollo, and the initial voyage toward Lemnos.

l: Argonauts’ return voyage, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: The return to Hellas is described as a journey shared by all the heroes after reaching Aeetes’ land. Jason asks Apollo to bring the ship and his comrades safely back, and Idmon prophesies that they will return with the fleece.

l: the sacrifice to Apollo, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Jason and the heroes build an altar to Apollo Actius and Embasius on the shore and sacrifice two steers. They burn the thigh bones in fat, pour libations, and pray for safe travel and a favorable wind.

l: Iolcus, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Iolcos is the homeland from which the heroes’ voyage begins. Jason is associated with its royal household, and the ship departs from the nearby shore of Pagasae.

l: Pagasae, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Pagasae is the beach and harbour where Argo lies ready and where the heroes assemble. They launch the ship there, sacrifice to Apollo, and sail away from the harbour.

l: Hellas, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Hellas is the homeland to which the heroes hope to return after reaching Aeetes’ land. Jason asks Apollo to bring the ship and comrades safely back to Hellas.

l: Mount Pelion, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Mount Pelion overlooks the departure route, and its nymphs watch the heroes wielding the oars. The Argonauts pass its rugged sides and the Sepian headland before continuing onward.

l: Lemnos, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: Lemnos, identified as the Sintian isle, is reached by the heroes after the wind fails at sunset. It is the last destination named in this unit.

l: the Argonauts’ departure from Iolcos, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: The Argonauts’ departure from Iolcos is prepared through Jason’s leadership, the launching of Argo at Pagasae, and the sacrifice to Apollo. They finally leave the harbour by rowing and sailing along the coast.

l: the launch of Argo, The Argonautica, Now when all things had been made ready by the thralls, all things that
s: The heroes dig a trench, place rollers beneath Argo, and push the ship into the sea using their strength and reversed oars. They then install the mast, sails, stores, and rowing benches before setting out.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The Lemnian women have slain the Lemnian men because the men rejected their lawful wives for captive maids from Thrace, though Hypsipyle spared her father Thoas. When Argo arrives, Hypsipyle and the Lemnian women’s assembly decide to receive the Minyae with gifts and invite them into the city, and Jason is welcomed by Hypsipyle. The Argonauts remain on Lemnos until Heracles reproaches them and urges departure, after which they sail onward toward the Hellespont while Jason and Hypsipyle part with promises concerning a possible child. The unit also describes Jason’s splendid mantle, the Argonauts’ rites at the island of Electra, and their continued voyage past Thracian and other shores.

l: Lemnian men, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The Lemnian men rejected their lawful wives and took captive maids brought from Thrace. The Lemnian women slew all the men, including those with the captives, and the surviving men are said to dwell on the snowy tilths of Thrace.

l: Lemnian women, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The Lemnian women killed the men of their people and thereafter tended cattle, wore bronze armour, and worked the fields. They feared the return of the Thracians, welcomed the Minyae, entertained them in their homes, and lamented when the Argonauts departed.

l: Hypsipyle, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, alone spared her aged father during the massacre and became queen after Thoas was presumed dead. She summoned the Lemnian women’s assembly, proposed sending gifts to the Minyae, welcomed Jason, concealed the full truth of the killings, and parted from him tearfully while offering him Lemnos and her father’s sceptre if he returned.

l: Thoas, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Thoas was king over the Lemnian people and was spared by Hypsipyle. She sent him away in a hollow chest, and fishermen brought him to Oenoe, an island later called Sicinus after Sicinus, whom Oenoe bore to Thoas.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Jason was sent by the Minyae to answer Hypsipyle’s invitation and entered the city wearing a splendid mantle made by Athena. He declined the sovereignty of Lemnos, returned to the ship after speaking with Hypsipyle, and later promised that if their male child survived, it could be sent to Iolcus to aid his parents.

l: Minyae, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The Minyae arrived at Lemnos aboard Argo and accepted the invitation conveyed by Iphinoe. They entered the city, received hospitality from the Lemnian women, delayed their voyage, and finally prepared to leave after Heracles reproached them.

l: Heracles, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Heracles stayed behind with a few chosen comrades when the other Argonauts went to the city. He later gathered the men and reproached them for remaining with the Lemnian women, persuading them to prepare for departure.

l: Cypris, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Cypris brought terrible wrath upon the Lemnian men because they had long grudged her due honours. Her influence caused their destructive passion for captive maids, and she later stirred sweet desire among the Lemnian women so that Lemnos would again be inhabited by men.

l: Lemnos, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Lemnos was the island where the Lemnian men were massacred and where the Lemnian women received the Minyae. Hypsipyle described it as a fertile island and offered Jason its sovereignty, while the Argonauts later departed from it.

l: Thrace, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Thrace supplied the captive maids whom the Lemnian men brought back from their raids. After the conflict, the Lemnian men were said to live and plough fields in Thrace, and the Argonauts later sailed with Thracian land on one side.

l: Thracians, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The Thracians were the people raided by the Lemnian men and were feared by the Lemnian women as possible attackers. The Lemnian women watched the sea anxiously for their arrival, and Hypsipyle falsely told Jason that the Lemnian men were living among the Thracians.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Argo approached Lemnos while being rowed, prompting the armed Lemnian women to rush to the beach. After the stay on Lemnos, Argus loosed Argo’s hawsers and the ship carried the Argonauts onward past the island of Electra and through the Hellespont.

l: golden fleece, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The golden fleece remained the object the Argonauts were seeking. Hypsipyle prayed that Jason would return safely with it and deliver it to the king.

l: golden fleece quest, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The fleece quest caused Jason and the Minyae to continue their journey despite the comfort and marriage prospects offered on Lemnos. Heracles warned that staying with the Lemnian women would bring no fair renown or fleece, and the Argonauts resumed their voyage.

l: the Lemnian massacre, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The Lemnian massacre was carried out by the women after the men rejected their lawful wives for captive maids. The women killed the husbands and captives together with all other males, while Hypsipyle alone saved Thoas; Hypsipyle later concealed this deed from Jason.

l: Argonauts’ return voyage, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: During the Argonauts’ voyage, the crew stopped at Lemnos, delayed their departure through feasting and relationships with the Lemnian women, and then sailed on after Heracles intervened. They visited the island of Electra for rites, crossed waters near Thrace and Imbros, passed the Chersonesus and several named shores, and entered the Hellespont.

l: the Lemnian women’s assembly, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: Hypsipyle summoned the Lemnian women’s assembly and proposed sending the Minyae food and wine while keeping them outside the towers. Polyxo instead urged the women to entrust their homes, livestock, and city to the strangers for protection and future children, and the assembly approved the plan.

l: the Lemnian women’s alliance with the Argonauts, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The Lemnian women’s alliance with the Argonauts began when they sent gifts and invited the men into the city. The women then hosted the Argonauts in their homes, but the alliance ended when Heracles urged the men to resume the voyage.

l: the marriage-bed conflict, The Argonautica, Here the whole of the men of the people together had been ruthlessly
s: The marriage-bed conflict began when the Lemnian men rejected their lawful wives and desired captive maids from Thrace. The conflict brought dishonour to lawful children, neglect to unmarried maidens and widowed mothers, and ultimately the Lemnian massacre.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Argo reaches the Mount of Bears in the Propontis, where the Argonauts and the Doliones initially welcome one another, but a nighttime misunderstanding leads to a battle in which Cyzicus and many others are killed. The Minyan heroes mourn Cyzicus and his wife Cleite, who takes her own life, while the Doliones endure profound grief. A twelve-day storm delays the Argo until Mopsus interprets a halcyon’s cry as a command to sacrifice to the Mother of the gods on Dindymum. Jason and the heroes perform the sacrifice to Rhea, the winds cease, and the Argo resumes its voyage, though Heracles later breaks his oar.

l: Propontis, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Propontis contains the lofty island called the Mount of Bears, near the Phrygian mainland and the river Aesepus.

l: Mount of Bears, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Mount of Bears is the island where the Doliones dwell near the isthmus and where the Earthborn live. The Argonauts fight the Earthborn there, later mistakenly return there at night, and perform sacrifices to Rhea on its mountain.

l: Earthborn, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Earthborn are fierce six-handed monsters living on the Mount of Bears. They attack the Argo at Chytus, but Heracles and the other heroes kill them all.

l: Doliones, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Doliones inhabit the isthmus and plain around the Mount of Bears under Cyzicus. They welcome the heroes, then mistakenly fight them when the Argo returns at night, suffering many deaths and later mourning Cyzicus.

l: Cyzicus son of Aeneus, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Cyzicus son of Aeneus is king of the Doliones and welcomes Jason and the heroes with hospitality. During the nighttime battle caused by mistaken identities, Jason strikes and kills him.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Argo reaches the Fair Haven, sails to Chytus, and later returns by contrary winds to the Doliones. It remains delayed by a twelve-day storm, then sails onward after the sacrifice to Rhea; during the voyage Heracles breaks his oar.

l: Thrace, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Winds from Thrace drive the Argo toward the Mount of Bears. The heroes later row to the Thracian harbour before climbing Dindymum.

l: Pelias, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Pelias is mentioned as the source of the injunction governing the heroes’ quest, which Cyzicus asks Jason about.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Jason leads the heroes in their dealings with the Doliones and kills Cyzicus during the nighttime battle without recognizing him. He accepts Mopsus’s prophecy, climbs Dindymum, and beseeches the Mother of the gods to end the storm.

l: Cleite, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Cleite is the young wife of Cyzicus, daughter of Percosian Merops. After Cyzicus dies, she hangs herself, and the nymphs’ tears for her become the fountain called Cleite.

l: Dindymum, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Dindymum is the mountain the heroes climb to survey the sea and later ascend to propitiate the Mother of the gods. A sacred image and altar are established there, and a new spring called the spring of Jason flows from its peak.

l: Hera, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Hera is said to have nurtured the Earthborn to make them a trial for Heracles.

l: Minyan heroes, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Minyan heroes fight the Earthborn and later mistakenly battle the Doliones at night. They mourn Cyzicus for three days, perform funeral rites and games, and participate in the sacrifice on Dindymum.

l: Argonauts, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Argonauts are welcomed by Cyzicus and the Doliones, defeat the Earthborn, and accidentally kill Cyzicus and other Doliones during their nighttime return. They endure the storm, sacrifice to Rhea, and continue sailing.

l: Cyzicus’s death, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Cyzicus’s death occurs during the mistaken nighttime battle between the Doliones and the returning heroes. Jason strikes him in the breast, and the Minyan heroes and Doliones mourn him for three days before holding funeral rites and games.

l: Cleite’s suicide, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Cleite’s suicide follows the death of her husband Cyzicus. She places a noose around her neck, and her death is mourned by the nymphs, whose tears form the fountain called Cleite.

l: twelve-day storm, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The twelve-day storm keeps the Argo from sailing after the funeral rites. It ends after Mopsus interprets the halcyon’s cry and directs Jason to sacrifice to the Mother of the gods.

l: Mopsus, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Mopsus son of Ampycus keeps watch with Acastus and understands the halcyon’s cry as a favorable omen. He wakes Jason and tells him to climb Dindymum and propitiate the Mother of the gods so the storm will cease.

l: Mother of the gods, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The Mother of the gods is honored on Dindymum as the power governing the winds, sea, earth, and Olympus. Jason and the heroes build an image and altar for her and offer sacrifices that bring favorable signs and end the storm.

l: Rhea, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Rhea is invoked as the venerable mother of Dindymum and the goddess dwelling in Phrygia. The heroes sacrifice to her with prayers, libations, armed dancing, and the clashing of shields, after which the winds cease and nature becomes abundant.

l: Cyzicus, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Cyzicus is killed by Jason during the accidental battle between the heroes and the Doliones. His death causes the mourning of both peoples and leads to funeral rites, games, and yearly libations by the Ionians at his city.

l: Heracles, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: Heracles kills Earthborn attackers with his bow and helps lead the slaughter of the monsters. He later kills Telecles and Megabrontes, rows with great strength after the storm, and breaks his oar while the Argo approaches the Mysian mainland.

l: battle of the Doliones and Argonauts, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The battle begins when the returning heroes and the Doliones mistake each other for hostile Pelasgian war-men and attack at night. Cyzicus and many Doliones die, as do several champions among the heroes, and the error is recognized at dawn.

l: sacrifice to Rhea, The Argonautica, There is a lofty island inside the Propontis, a short distance from the
s: The sacrifice to Rhea takes place on rugged Dindymum after Mopsus’s prophecy. The heroes make a wooden image, heap an altar, offer libations and sacrifices, and dance in armor; favorable signs appear, a spring rises, and the storm ends.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Heracles and his companions reach the land of the Cianians, where the Mysians welcome them and provide food, wine, and lodging. While Heracles cuts a pine for an oar, Hylas goes to the spring called Pegae, where a water-nymph abducts him. Polyphemus son of Eilatus hears Hylas’s cry, but Heracles’s search fails, and the Argonaut ship sails away with Heracles and Hylas left behind. Glaucus explains that their separation is ordained by Zeus, after which Jason and Telamon reconcile and the remaining heroes continue their voyage.

l: Heracles, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Heracles reaches the Cianian land with the heroes and goes into the woods to cut a pine for an oar. After learning from Polyphemus son of Eilatus that Hylas is missing, he abandons the pine and searches for him in a frenzy. Glaucus says that Heracles is destined to return to Argos, perform twelve labors for Eurystheus, and later dwell with the immortals; Heracles also threatens to lay waste to the Mysian land unless Hylas’s fate is discovered.

l: Hylas, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Hylas carries a bronze pitcher to Pegae to draw water for the evening meal and prepare everything for Heracles’s return. A water-nymph sees him, pulls him into the spring, and makes him her husband according to Glaucus’s account. The Mysians later give pledges that they will continue searching for him.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Jason remains silent and grief-stricken when the heroes realize that Heracles and Hylas have been left behind. After Telamon accuses him of arranging Heracles’s abandonment, Jason later accepts Telamon’s apology and restores their friendship.

l: Polyphemus, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Polyphemus hears Hylas’s cry near Pegae and searches for him, fearing that wild beasts or ambushers have taken him. He meets Heracles on the path and tells him that Hylas has disappeared. Glaucus says that Polyphemus is destined to found a city at the mouth of Cius among the Mysians.

l: Telamon, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Telamon angrily accuses Jason of leaving Heracles behind and nearly leads the heroes back toward the Mysian land. After Glaucus explains the divine purpose of the separation, Telamon admits his fault and asks Jason to forgive him, and the two are reconciled.

l: Minyan heroes, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: The heroes are hospitably welcomed by the Mysians and receive provisions, sheep, wine, firewood, bedding, and a feast after sacrificing to Apollo Ecbasius. They sail away before realizing that Heracles and Hylas have been left behind, then quarrel violently over the abandonment. After Glaucus’s explanation and the reconciliation of Jason and Telamon, they continue their voyage.

l: Mysians, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: The Mysians welcome the heroes to their land and provide them with food, sheep, wine, firewood, bedding, and hospitality. After Heracles threatens their land, they choose noble sons as pledges and swear to continue searching for Hylas. They also send youths from Cius as pledges, whom Heracles settles at Trachis.

l: Cius, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Cius is associated with the Mysian land near the Arganthonian mount and the outfall of Cius. Glaucus says that Polyphemus is destined to found a city at the mouth of Cius, and the people of Cius later send youths as pledges in the search for Hylas.

l: Pegae, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Pegae is the spring near which Hylas goes to draw water. The water-nymphs hold their dances there while honoring Artemis, and the water-nymph abducts Hylas into its eddy.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: The Argonaut ship is urged onward by Tiphys when the morning star rises. Its anchors and ropes are drawn up, its sails fill with wind, and it carries the heroes away from the Mysian coast while Heracles and Hylas remain behind. Later, the ship reaches a broad beach by rowing when the wind dies.

l: Hylas’s bronze pitcher, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Hylas’s bronze pitcher is carried to Pegae so that Hylas can draw water for the evening meal. As he dips it into the spring, the ringing sound of the water against the bronze accompanies the water-nymph’s attack.

l: Hylas’s abduction by the water-nymph, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Hylas’s abduction occurs at Pegae when the water-nymph, overcome by desire for his beauty, pulls him into the spring as he draws water. Glaucus later says that the goddess-nymph makes Hylas her husband, causing Heracles and Polyphemus to wander and be left behind.

l: the water-nymph, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: The water-nymph rises from the fair-flowing spring at Pegae and sees Hylas in the moonlight. Cypris makes her heart faint with desire, and she pulls Hylas into the eddy while he is drawing water. Glaucus says that she makes Hylas her husband.

l: the Argonauts’ abandonment of Heracles and Hylas, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: The Argonauts’ abandonment of Heracles and Hylas occurs when Tiphys urges the ship to depart before the missing men return. At dawn the heroes realize that they have sailed away without them, causing a fierce quarrel. Glaucus explains that their separation follows the counsel of Zeus and the destined fates of Heracles, Polyphemus, and Hylas.

l: Heracles’ labors for Eurystheus, The Argonautica, Now at the hour when from the field some delver or ploughman goes
s: Heracles’ labors for Eurystheus are presented as his destined future after he is left behind in the Mysian land. Glaucus says that Heracles must return to Argos, complete twelve labors, and then dwell with the immortals if he fulfills the remaining ones.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: Amycus, king of the Bebrycians, forces the Argonauts to accept his boxing challenge, and Polydeuces defeats and kills him. When the Bebrycians attack in retaliation, the Argonaut heroes repel them while Lycus and the Mariandyni ravage Bebrycian lands. The Argonauts tend their wounded, sacrifice and feast, then sail through the Bosporus, where Tiphys safely steers the ship past a terrifying storm.

l: Amycus, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: Amycus is the haughty king of the Bebrycians and imposes a rule that no stranger may depart without boxing him. He fights Polydeuces but is defeated when Polydeuces strikes him above the ear, breaking the bones inside his head.

l: Bebrycians, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: The Bebrycians are ruled by Amycus and are required to obey his boxing ordinance. After Amycus dies, they attack Polydeuces and his comrades, but the Argonaut heroes drive them inland and they flee while their lands are being ravaged by Lycus and the Mariandyni.

l: Polydeuces, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: Polydeuces accepts Amycus's boxing challenge as champion of his comrades. He skillfully withstands Amycus's attacks, kills him with a blow above the ear, and later kills Itymoneus and Mimas during the fighting with the Bebrycians.

l: Minyan heroes, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: The Argonaut heroes support Polydeuces in the fight against the Bebrycians. Castor, Ancaeus, Jason, the sons of Aeacus, and others help rout the Bebrycians, after which the heroes tend their wounded, sacrifice to the immortals, feast, and sail onward.

l: Bebrycia, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: Bebrycia is the land of Amycus and the Bebrycians. After Amycus's death, its vineyards, villages, steadings, and farms are ravaged by Lycus, the Mariandyni, and the departing heroes.

l: Bosporus, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: The Argonauts steer through the eddying Bosporus after leaving the coast of the Bebrycians. They encounter a wave rising like a mountain but pass through safely by Tiphys's skill.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: The Argonauts' ship carries the heroes away from the land of the Bebrycians with their needed spoil aboard. It passes through the Bosporus and survives the great wave without harm.

l: Amycus's boxing challenge, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: Amycus's challenge requires every stranger visiting the Bebrycians to fight him in boxing before departing. Polydeuces willingly accepts it, and the challenge ends with Amycus's defeat and death.

l: Amycus’s boxing match and death, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: Amycus dies when Polydeuces evades his descending blow and strikes him above the ear, breaking the bones inside his head. His death causes the Bebrycians to attack the Argonauts, while Lycus and the Mariandyni assault Bebrycian territory.

l: attack on the Bebrycians, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: After Amycus dies, the Bebrycians rush Polydeuces with clubs and spears. The Argonaut heroes counterattack, kill several Bebrycians, and drive the survivors inland.

l: the Bosporus storm, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: A wave like a steep mountain rises before the Argonauts' ship in the Bosporus and appears to threaten it with destruction. The ship escapes the storm safely through the steering skill of Tiphys.

l: Tiphys, The Argonautica, BOOK II
s: Tiphys pilots the Argonauts' ship through the Bosporus. By his steering skill, he brings the ship safely past the enormous wave, leaving the heroes unharmed though greatly frightened.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Phineus, son of Agenor, is tormented by blindness, old age, and the Harpies, which continually steal and foul his food. Zetes and Calais, the sons of Boreas, drive the Harpies away, but Iris prevents them from killing the creatures and swears that they will not return. Phineus then foretells the Argonauts’ route through the Cyanean rocks and Pontus to Aea, describing the dangers and landmarks leading to the Golden Fleece. After receiving his guidance, Jason and the Argonauts prepare to continue their voyage when the Etesian winds begin to blow.

l: Phineus, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Phineus, son of Agenor, lives by the sea and suffers blindness, extreme old age, weakness, and the Harpies’ theft of his food. He welcomes Jason and the Argonauts, gives them prophetic directions for their voyage, and advises them to seek the aid of the Cyprian goddess.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Jason leads the Argonauts on the Argo in search of the Golden Fleece. He and the other heroes help Phineus, listen to his instructions, and ask how they will return from Aea.

l: Zeus, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Zeus punishes Phineus with lingering old age and the loss of his sight because Phineus revealed his sacred will too fully. Zeus also gives Zetes and Calais tireless strength during their pursuit of the Harpies.

l: Zetes, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Zetes, one of the sons of Boreas, promises to help Phineus after receiving his oath that heaven will not punish him and Calais. He and Calais chase the Harpies, and Zetes later reports to the heroes how Iris stopped them from killing the creatures.

l: Calais, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Calais, one of the sons of Boreas, helps drive the Harpies away from Phineus. He pursues them with Zetes nearly to the Floating Islands before Iris intervenes.

l: Iris, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Iris stops Zetes and Calais from striking the Harpies, declaring that they are the hounds of Zeus. She swears by the waters of Styx that the Harpies will never again approach Phineus’s home.

l: Aeetes, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Aeetes is associated with the towers of Cytaean Aea, which Phineus says the Argonauts will see when they reach the river Phasis.

l: Cyprian goddess, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Phineus tells the Argonauts to rely on the artful aid of the Cyprian goddess, saying that the glorious outcome of their venture depends on her.

l: Harpies, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Harpies swoop from the clouds to snatch food from Phineus’s mouth and hands, leaving behind an intolerable stench. Zetes and Calais chase them away, and Iris’s oath ensures that they will not return to Phineus.

l: Argonauts, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Argonauts are the band of Greek chiefs whom Jason leads aboard the Argo in quest of the Golden Fleece. They aid Phineus, receive his prophecy, and prepare to pass through the Cyanean rocks and sail onward to Aea.

l: sons of Boreas, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The sons of Boreas, Zetes and Calais, are destined by an oracle to restrain the Harpies. They drive the creatures away from Phineus but return after Iris swears that the Harpies will not come back.

l: Colchians, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Colchians live beyond the Sapeires and Byzeres, near the end of the Argonauts’ route. Phineus identifies them as the people of the region containing Aea and the Golden Fleece.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Argo carries Jason and the Argonauts toward the Golden Fleece. Phineus warns that even an iron Argo could not escape the Cyanean rocks without obeying the proper omen.

l: golden fleece, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Golden Fleece is the object of Jason’s expedition. Phineus says it lies in the grove of Ares near Cytaean Aea, spread upon an oak and guarded by a sleepless dragon.

l: dove, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Phineus instructs the Argonauts to send a dove between the Cyanean rocks before attempting the passage themselves. If the dove survives, they should follow; if it perishes, they must turn back.

l: oracle, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: An oracle declares that the sons of Boreas will restrain the Harpies. It also reveals to Phineus that the Argonauts’ arrival will bring him relief from their attacks.

l: Phineus’s punishment, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Phineus’s punishment consists of lingering old age, blindness, weakness, and the continual loss and pollution of his food. Zeus imposes it because Phineus revealed divine will too completely.

l: Harpies’ attack on Phineus, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Harpies repeatedly descend upon Phineus’s meals, snatching away nearly all the food and fouling what remains with a dreadful stench. Their attacks force him to eat despite the contamination and leave him in continual misery.

l: chase of the Harpies, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: After the Harpies attack Phineus’s prepared feast, Zetes and Calais pursue them over the sea. They nearly overtake them at the Floating Islands, but Iris descends and prevents the Harpies’ destruction.

l: Iris’s oath, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Iris swears by the waters of Styx that the Harpies will never again approach the home of Phineus. The oath causes Zetes and Calais to abandon their pursuit and return to the ship.

l: Argonauts’ voyage, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Phineus foretells that the Argonauts will pass the Cyanean rocks, enter Pontus, follow the coasts and rivers of the region, and eventually reach Aea. He describes the landmarks and peoples they will encounter, while warning them to obey divine signs.

l: Floating Islands, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Floating Islands are where Zetes and Calais nearly overtake the Harpies. After Iris’s intervention, the heroes turn back from them.

l: Islands of Turning, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Floating Islands are thereafter called the Islands of Turning because Zetes and Calais turn back there after Iris gives her oath. They were previously known as the Floating Islands.

l: Pontus, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Phineus tells the Argonauts to enter Pontus after surviving the Cyanean rocks. He gives them directions for sailing along its shores toward the lands of the Colchians and Aea.

l: Cyanean rocks, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The twin Cyanean rocks clash together where two seas meet, throwing up salt water and making passage extremely dangerous. Phineus instructs the Argonauts to test the route with a dove before attempting it with the Argo.

l: Aea, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Aea is the distant destination at the edge of Pontus and the world, where the Argonauts will find the Golden Fleece. Phineus says that a deity will guide their return from Aea by another route.

l: Cytaean mainland, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: The Cytaean mainland is where the Argonauts will reach the river Phasis and see the towers of Cytaean Aea. Near it lies the grove of Ares containing the Golden Fleece.

l: Phasis, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: Phasis flows broadly from the Cytaean mainland toward the sea. Phineus directs the Argonauts to guide the Argo to its mouth.

l: serpent guarding the fleece, The Argonautica, There Phineus, son of Agenor, had his home by the sea, Phineus who
s: A terrible dragon guards the Golden Fleece, which is spread upon an oak in the grove of Ares. The dragon keeps watch constantly, since sweet sleep never overcomes its eyes.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: The Argonauts, guided by Phineus's counsel, escape the Cyanean rocks with Athena's aid and continue along the Bithynian coast. After Apollo appears on Thynia, they sacrifice to him, establish an altar, sing and dance, and swear an oath of mutual aid. They then reach the Acherusian headland and the land of the Mariandyni, where Lycus and his people welcome them because Polydeuces slew Amycus and defeated the Bebrycians. Lycus hears Jason recount the expedition, mourns the loss of Heracles, gives the Argonauts gifts, and sends his son Dascylus with them.

l: Apollo, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Apollo carried Cyrene from Haemonia to Libya, made her a long-lived huntress-nymph, and fathered Aristaeus by her. He commanded Aristaeus to go to Ceos to ward off the pestilence caused by Sirius. Apollo later appeared to the Argonauts on Thynia with a silver bow and quiver, passing through the air toward the sea; they sacrificed to him and sang of his slaying of Delphyne.

l: Sirius, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Sirius scorched the Minoan Isles for a long time, causing pestilence and giving the inhabitants no respite. Aristaeus, by Apollo's command, established rites to Sirius and Zeus on Ceos, after which Etesian winds cooled the land for forty days.

l: Zeus, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Aristaeus built a great altar to Zeus Icmaeus on Ceos and offered sacrifices to Zeus and Sirius. The Argonauts later raised an altar to the blessed twelve on the shore of Thynia.

l: Thynians, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: While the chieftains were held at Thynia by constraint, the Thynians sent them gifts beyond measure to please Phineus.

l: Phineus, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: The Thynians gave gifts to the chieftains in order to please Phineus. His prophecy that the Argonauts' later toils would be lightly accomplished encouraged Jason after their escape from the Cyanean rocks.

l: Argonauts, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: The Argonauts received gifts from the Thynians, raised an altar to the blessed twelve, and entered Argo carrying a trembling dove. They escaped the Cyanean rocks, sacrificed to Apollo on Thynia, swore mutual aid, and continued to the land of the Mariandyni, where Lycus welcomed them and sent Dascylus with them.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Argo passed between the Cyanean rocks after Athena thrust one rock back and pushed the ship through. The rocks tore away part of the ship's stern-ornament, but Argo escaped and continued along the sea.

l: Euphemus, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Euphemus carried the trembling dove to the prow and released her to test the passage between the Cyanean rocks. After her tail-feathers were clipped by the rocks, he urged the rowers to bend to their oars with all their strength.

l: Athena, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Athena aided the Argonauts by setting her foot on a cloud and hastening to the shore of Thynia. During the passage between the Cyanean rocks, she thrust back one rock and pushed Argo through, after which she rose to Olympus.

l: Thynia, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Thynia was the place where the Argonauts were constrained while the Thynians brought them gifts, and where Athena came to aid them. On its shore Apollo appeared at dawn, and the Argonauts built an altar, offered sacrifices, danced, sang, and swore an oath of concord.

l: Cyanean rocks, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: The Cyanean rocks clashed together and nearly destroyed Argo as the Argonauts tried to pass between them. The dove escaped with only the end of her tail-feathers torn away, and Athena forced Argo through; afterward the rocks became rooted together forever.

l: Tiphys, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Tiphys, son of Hagnias, directed the rowing through the Cyanean rocks and eased Argo as a huge wave threatened the ship. After the escape, he reassured Jason that Athena had given Argo divine strength and that Phineus had foretold easier labors ahead.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Jason confessed that he regretted not refusing Pelias's command and feared for himself, his comrades, and their return to Hellas. Encouraged by the chiefs' cheering words, he regained courage and said he would no longer fear even the gulfs of Hades. At Lycus's palace he recounted the expedition and the events that had brought the Argonauts to the Mariandyni.

l: Pelias, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Pelias commanded Jason to undertake the quest. Jason later said that he should have refused Pelias's command, even if refusal had led to a pitiless death.

l: Orpheus, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Orpheus urged the Argonauts to call Thynia the sacred isle of Apollo of the Dawn, to build an altar, and to offer sacrifices if Apollo granted them a safe return. He led the singing of a hymn to Apollo and played a clear lay on his Bistonian lyre about Apollo's slaying of Delphyne.

l: Mariandyni, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: The Argonauts reached the land of the Mariandyni after passing the river Sangarius, Lycus, and the Anthemoeisian lake. The Mariandyni welcomed them with Lycus because Polydeuces had slain Amycus and the people had long been at war with the Bebrycians.

l: Lycus, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Lycus, lord of the Mariandyni, welcomed the Argonauts and listened as Jason recounted their journey. He praised Heracles, explained the harm done to his land by the Bebrycians, thanked the Argonauts for punishing them, offered gifts, and sent his son Dascylus with the expedition.

l: Acherusian headland, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: The Acherusian headland rose in steep cliffs above the Bithynian sea and contained a cave of Hades, an icy breath, and the outfall of the river Acheron. The Argonauts reached it after the wind ceased and came ashore opposite it; Lycus promised to build a lofty temple to the sons of Tyndareus on its height.

l: Bebrycians, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: The Bebrycians had long warred against the Mariandyni and had cut off large parts of Lycus's land, extending their boundary to the meadows of the Hypius. The Argonauts, through the hands of Polydeuces and their other companions, made the Bebrycians pay for their actions.

l: Polydeuces, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Polydeuces slew Amycus, the champion of the Bebrycians, in a boxing match. The Mariandyni welcomed Polydeuces like a god because he and the Argonauts had helped them against the Bebrycians.

l: Amycus, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Amycus was the arrogant champion of the Bebrycians. Polydeuces killed him in a boxing match, and Lycus said that this defeat had brought the Bebrycians' punishment.

l: Heracles, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Heracles had been left behind in the Mysian land at Cius, against the Argonauts' will. Lycus grieved that the Argonauts had lost his help and recalled Heracles's earlier deeds in Asia, including his victory over Titias and his subjugation of neighboring peoples.

l: Amycus’s boxing match and death, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Polydeuces entered a boxing match with Amycus and slew the Bebrycian champion. The death of Amycus helped end the Bebrycians' oppression of the Mariandyni, who consequently made a league with the Argonauts.

l: crossing of the Cyanean rocks, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: During the crossing, the dove passed between the rocks, which then crashed together and tore away the end of her tail-feathers. A great wave, the current, and the clashing rocks threatened Argo, but Tiphys's steering, the rowers' strength, and Athena's intervention carried the ship through; afterward the rocks were fixed together forever.

l: Apollo’s appearance on Thynias, The Argonautica, Cyrene, the tale goes, once tended sheep along the marsh-meadow of
s: Apollo appeared to the Argonauts at dawn on Thynia as he traveled from Lycia toward the Hyperboreans, with golden hair, a silver bow, and a quiver. The island quaked beneath him and the waves surged, while the Argonauts bowed without daring to look directly at him; afterward they sacrificed and dedicated the island to Apollo of the Dawn.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Idmon, son of Abas, is killed by a white-tusked boar, and Tiphys, son of Hagnias, dies soon afterward from a short sickness. The Argonauts mourn and bury both men with honours, then Ancaeus takes up the steering of the Argo after Hera gives him courage. During the voyage they pass many lands and peoples, including the Amazons and the Chalybes, and reach the island of Ares, where the birds of Ares attack them. Following Amphidamas’ advice, they defend themselves with locked shields, spears, helmets, and loud noise, causing the birds to flee.

l: Peleus, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Peleus attacks the murderous boar with his hunting spear after it wounds Idmon. Later, he urges the grieving heroes to resume their voyage and calls on them to trust the remaining steersmen.

l: Acheron, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The river Acheron is the place where Idmon is killed and where Tiphys dies after the Argonauts bury Idmon. The Argonauts later sail out through its river mouth.

l: Ancaeus, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Hera gives Ancaeus exceeding courage, and he urges Peleus and the others not to abandon their voyage. Ancaeus, who is skilled in steering, undertakes to guide the Argo.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Jason is identified as Aeson’s son. He expresses fear that the Argonauts will die without reaching the city of Aeetes or returning to Hellas, but he accepts the plan to continue when Ancaeus takes the helm.

l: Hera, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Hera kindles exceeding courage in Ancaeus when the Argonauts are overcome by grief after the deaths of Idmon and Tiphys.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The Argo leaves the river Acheron on the twelfth day with a strong westerly wind. It passes many rivers, headlands, islands, and peoples, and reaches the island of Ares, where it is attacked by birds.

l: Amazons, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The Amazons are described as warlike daughters of Ares and the nymph Harmonia who dwell in three scattered tribes. The Argonauts land near the outfall of Thermodon but leave when the wind rises, avoiding battle with the Amazons.

l: Thermodon, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The Thermodon flows into the sea near the bay where the Argonauts come ashore. It is described as a vast river whose many streams spread over the land before entering the Pontus.

l: island of Ares, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The island of Ares lies near the route of the Argo and is inhabited by hostile birds. The Argonauts reach it after passing the Mossynoeci, and the birds attack them as they approach.

l: birds of Ares, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The birds of Ares attack the Argo by shooting sharp feathers from the air. One feather wounds Oileus, while Clytius kills one bird with an arrow; when the heroes reach the island and clash their shields, the birds rise in countless numbers and flee toward the opposite mountains.

l: Heracles, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Heracles had previously encountered birds on the Stymphalian lake and drove them away by shaking a bronze rattle and making a loud clatter. Amphidamas cites this as the model for defending the Argonauts against the birds of Ares.

l: Ares’s birds’ attack, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The attack wounds Oileus when a feather strikes his left shoulder and forces him to drop his oar. The heroes respond with helmets, shields, spears, and loud noise, after which the birds withdraw.

l: Idmon’s death, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Idmon’s death occurs when a white-tusked boar charges from the reeds and tears through his thigh. The Argonauts lament him for three days, bury him with full honours, and raise a barrow marked by a flourishing wild olive tree.

l: Tiphys’s death, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Tiphys’s death follows Idmon’s burial, when a short sickness lays him to rest far from his homeland. The Argonauts bury him near Idmon and initially lose all hope of continuing the voyage.

l: funeral rites for Idmon and Tiphys, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The Argonauts lament Idmon for three days before burying him with full honours, while the people and King Lycus join the rites and countless sheep are slaughtered at his tomb. They also bury Tiphys near the seer after paying due honours to him.

l: Argonauts’ voyage, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: The Argonauts resume their voyage after the deaths of Idmon and Tiphys, sailing from Acheron through fair weather and passing numerous rivers, headlands, islands, and foreign peoples. They reach the land of the Amazons, continue past the Chalybes, Tibareni, and Mossynoeci, and approach the island of Ares.

l: Ares’s shield-and-noise defense, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Amphidamas advises the Argonauts to alternate rowing and shielding the ship, wear high-crested helmets, raise spears, and make a mighty noise. They lock their shields together over the ship and clash them on reaching the island, frightening the birds into flight.

l: Zeus, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: Zeus is said to have given Sinope, daughter of Asopus, a home and promised to grant her whatever she desired; she cleverly asked him for virginity. The headland of Genetaean Zeus is also passed safely during the voyage.

l: steering the Argo, The Argonautica, And here his destined fate smote Idmon, son of Abas, skilled in
s: After Tiphys dies, Ancaeus undertakes to steer the Argo, with Erginus, Nauplius, and Euphemus also offering their services. The others grant the task to Ancaeus, who guides the ship when the Argonauts resume sailing.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The sons of Phrixus are shipwrecked near the island of Ares and meet Jason and the heroes after a violent storm. Argus explains their lineage from Phrixus and their journey toward Orchomenus, while Jason recognizes them as relatives and asks them to guide the heroes to Aeetes and the golden fleece. After sacrificing at the temple of Ares, the combined company sails past Philyra, the Caucasian coast, and Prometheus until reaching the river Phasis and the land of Colchis. Jason makes offerings and, following Argus’s advice, anchors the ship in a shaded backwater to plan how to approach Aeetes.

l: Phineus, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Phineus had previously given prophecies whose fulfillment Jason believes is shown by the arrival of the sons of Phrixus.

l: sons of Phrixus, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The sons of Phrixus sail from Aea toward Orchomenus to claim their father’s wealth, but a storm destroys their Colchian ship near the island of Ares. They cling to a beam, reach the island alive, and meet Jason and the heroes. Argus identifies himself and his brothers as Cytissorus, Phrontis, and Melas, and explains their descent from Phrixus.

l: Phrixus, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Phrixus, an Aeolid, traveled from Hellas to Aea on a golden ram and was received by Aeetes, who married him to Chalciope. He later died in Aeetes’ house and instructed his sons to journey to Orchomenus to claim Athamas’s possessions. Jason says he is voyaging to atone for the intended sacrifice of Phrixus, which caused Zeus’s wrath against the sons of Aeolus.

l: Aea, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Aea is the place from which the sons of Phrixus sail toward Orchomenus and the city associated with Aeetes. It lies beside the river Phasis, near the Caucasus and the grove of Ares.

l: Aeetes, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Cytaean Aeetes is the ruler whose city and household receive Phrixus and whose possession of the golden fleece is the goal of Jason’s voyage. Argus fears that Aeetes will resist any attempt to take the fleece.

l: Zeus, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Zeus sends the north wind and storm that wreck the sons of Phrixus’ ship, then causes the rain to cease at sunrise. He is invoked as the god of strangers and suppliants, and Jason credits him with rescuing Phrixus and his sons.

l: island of Ares, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The island of Ares is where the storm-driven sons of Phrixus come ashore and meet the heroes. The company sacrifices at a temple of Ares there, then sails away at dawn.

l: Argus, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Argus asks Jason and the heroes for shelter after the shipwreck and recounts the history and names of the sons of Phrixus. He warns that Aeetes, the Colchians, and the sleepless serpent make the recovery of the golden fleece extremely difficult. Later, Jason follows Argus’s advice by anchoring the ship in a shaded backwater near the river Phasis.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Jason questions Argus, recognizes the sons of Phrixus as relatives, gives them clothing, and welcomes them aboard the heroes’ ship. He asks them to help guide the voyage to recover the golden fleece and says that he is seeking to atone for the intended sacrifice of Phrixus. At the river Phasis, he makes offerings to Earth, the local gods, and dead heroes before anchoring to plan the approach to Aeetes.

l: golden fleece, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The golden fleece is the fleece of the ram that carried Phrixus to Aea, and it hangs on an oak in the sacred grove of Ares. Jason and the heroes are eager to bring it to Hellas, although Argus warns that Aeetes and a deathless serpent guard it.

l: golden ram, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The golden ram carried Phrixus from Hellas to Aea and was made entirely of gold by Hermes. Phrixus sacrificed it to Zeus, and its fleece remained in Aea.

l: Hellas, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Hellas is the homeland from which Phrixus traveled to Aea and to which Jason intends to bring the golden fleece. Jason and the heroes are also sailing from Hellas on this mission.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The Argonauts’ ship was built by Athena, whose work with Argus produced its timbers near the crest of Pelion. Jason offers its use to the shipwrecked sons of Phrixus, whose own vessel has been shattered. The ship carries the company past the coast of the Caucasus and into the river Phasis.

l: Minyae, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The Argonauts meet the shipwrecked sons of Phrixus, give them clothing, and sacrifice with them at the temple of Ares. They then sail together toward Aea to seek the golden fleece and reach the river Phasis.

l: Ares, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Ares has a temple and a sacred grove in the land near Aea. The heroes sacrifice sheep at the temple on the island of Ares, while the golden fleece hangs in the grove under the guard of a serpent.

l: serpent guarding the fleece, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: A huge serpent, described as deathless and sleepless, keeps watch around the golden fleece in the grove of Ares. Argus says that taking the fleece despite Aeetes will therefore be no easy task.

l: Caucasus, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The Caucasian mountains rise beside the route to Aea and the river Phasis. The heroes see Prometheus bound on the rocks there and hear his cries as an eagle feeds on his liver.

l: Phasis, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: Phasis is reached at night after the heroes pass the Caucasian mountains. It marks the utmost boundary of their sea journey and leads them into the Colchian land.

l: river Phasis, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The river Phasis carries the ship into the land of Colchis, with the Caucasus and the Cytaean city of Aea on one side and the plain and grove of Ares on the other. Jason pours offerings into the river and then anchors the ship in a nearby shaded backwater.

l: storm and shipwreck, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: A violent storm driven by Zeus’s north wind covers the sea with rain, darkness, and huge waves. It tears away the sails and breaks the ship of the sons of Phrixus in two, but the four men survive by clinging to a beam and are carried to the island of Ares.

l: Argonauts’ voyage, The Argonautica, What then was the purpose of Phineus in bidding the divine band of
s: The voyage to Colchis brings Jason and the heroes from Hellas toward Aea in search of the golden fleece. After recovering from the meeting with the sons of Phrixus, they sail past Philyra, the Macrones, the Becheiri, the Sapeires, and the Byzeres, then enter the river Phasis and prepare to approach Aeetes.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Hera and Athena ask Cypris to persuade Eros to make Medea, the daughter of Aeetes, fall in love with Jason so that she will help him obtain the golden fleece. Hera explains that she favors Jason because he once carried her, disguised as an old woman, across a flood, and she wants Pelias punished. Cypris finds Eros playing dice with Ganymedes and promises him a golden ball if he shoots Medea with his love-inspiring arrow. Eros takes his bow and quiver and travels down from Olympus toward the earth, where Jason and his companions are seeking the fleece.

l: Erato, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Erato is invoked to tell how Jason brought the fleece back to Iolcus with the aid of Medea's love. She is associated with Cypris and with charming unwedded maidens through love.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Jason, the son of Aeson, is in quest of the golden fleece with his companions on the river Phasis. Hera favors him because he once carried her, disguised as an old woman, across a raging flood, and she seeks to help him return to Iolcus.

l: Medea, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Medea is identified as the daughter of Aeetes and an enchantress. Hera and Athena plan to have Eros charm her with love for Jason so that she will aid his quest.

l: Argonauts, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: The heroes wait unobserved in ambush among thick reed-beds while seeking the golden fleece. They are described as Jason's comrades, whose safety and success concern Hera.

l: Hera, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Hera consults Athena about obtaining the fleece and proposes asking Cypris to make Medea love Jason. She tells Cypris that she favors Jason because he once helped her while she was disguised as an old woman, and she wants Pelias punished.

l: Athena, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Athena discusses possible plans with Hera for helping the heroes seize the fleece. She agrees to accompany Hera to Cypris, though she says she does not know the charms of desire.

l: Cypris, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Cypris agrees to ask her son Eros to charm Aeetes' daughter with love for Jason. She finds Eros in Zeus' orchard, promises him a beautiful golden ball in exchange for the task, and sends him toward the earth.

l: Eros, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Eros plays golden dice with Ganymedes and wins, leaving Ganymedes angry and empty-handed. After Cypris promises him Zeus' golden ball, he takes his bow and quiver and sets out to shoot Aeetes' daughter with a love-inspiring shaft.

l: Aeetes, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Aeetes is the king whose daughter is an enchantress and is being targeted by Eros's planned love-arrow. His golden fleece is sought by Jason and his companions.

l: Pelias, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Pelias sent Jason on the quest and is described by Hera as having escaped an evil doom. Hera wants him to pay for leaving her without sacrifice and for his outrage.

l: Iolcus, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Iolcus is the place to which Jason is expected to return with the golden fleece. Erato's opening invocation also describes the fleece as being brought back there with Medea's help.

l: Hellas, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Hellas is the destination to which Jason is expected to bring the golden fleece. Hera says that Medea's aid could enable Jason to win the fleece and return there.

l: Phasis, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: The river Phasis is where Jason and his comrades have moored their ship while pursuing the golden fleece.

l: Olympus, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Olympus contains Cypris's palace and the orchard of Zeus, where Cypris finds Eros. Eros then passes through Olympus's high gates and travels downward toward the earth.

l: golden fleece, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: The golden fleece is the object sought by Jason and the heroes in Aeetes' land. Hera and Athena devise a plan to obtain it through Medea's love and assistance.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: The Argo is not named in this unit; Jason and his comrades are said to have moored their ship on the river Phasis.

l: Love, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Medea's love for Jason is presented as the intended means of helping him obtain the golden fleece. Hera and Athena ask Cypris to cause this love, but its fulfillment has not yet occurred in the unit.

l: golden fleece quest, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Jason and his companions are pursuing the golden fleece after mooring their ship on the river Phasis. Hera, Athena, Cypris, and Eros begin arranging supernatural aid for the quest.

l: the fleece's theft and return to Hellas, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: The planned seizure of the golden fleece and its return to Hellas depend on Medea being charmed into helping Jason. The theft and return have not yet taken place in this unit.

l: the love arrow, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: The love arrow belongs to Eros, who is instructed to shoot Aeetes' daughter and charm her with love for Jason. Eros takes his bow and quiver and sets out to perform this task.

l: the plot to make Medea love Jason, The Argonautica, BOOK III
s: Hera and Athena propose that Cypris have Eros shoot Medea with a love arrow. Cypris promises Eros a golden ball made for Zeus in return for making Aeetes' daughter love Jason and help him win the fleece.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Jason and the Argonauts enter Aea and visit Aeetes’ palace to request the golden fleece, while Jason proposes winning it through speech rather than force. Aeetes angrily demands that Jason yoke his bronze-footed bulls, plough the field of Ares, sow serpent’s teeth, and kill the earthborn armed men that arise. Medea falls in love with Jason after Eros shoots her with an arrow, and she fears that Aeetes or the bulls will kill him. Argus suggests seeking Medea’s help because Hecate taught her the use of powerful magic herbs.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Jason leads the expedition’s delegation to Aeetes’ palace and asks for the golden fleece, offering friendship and military aid in return. Aeetes sets him the deadly contest of the bronze-footed bulls, serpent’s teeth, and earthborn armed men; Jason accepts because necessity compels him, though he is deeply troubled by the task.

l: Argonauts, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: The Argonauts meet in council and agree that Jason should approach Aeetes with words before resorting to force. After hearing the king’s challenge, they are discouraged, though several volunteer to face the danger and Argus proposes seeking Medea’s assistance.

l: Aeetes, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Aeetes receives Jason, the sons of Phrixus, Telamon, and Augeias in his palace, but becomes enraged when he learns that they seek the golden fleece. He demands that Jason complete a deadly agricultural and martial trial before he will surrender it.

l: Medea, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Medea, the daughter of Aeetes and priestess of Hecate, sees Jason and falls helplessly in love with him after Eros shoots her. She fears for Jason’s life and mourns him as though Aeetes or the bronze-footed bulls have already killed him.

l: golden fleece, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: The golden fleece is the object of Jason’s quest, which Aeetes believes the visitors seek in order to seize his power. Aeetes promises to give it to Jason only if he completes the required contest.

l: contest of the bronze-footed bulls, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Aeetes’ contest requires Jason to yoke two bronze-footed, fire-breathing bulls, plough four furrows of the field of Ares, sow serpent’s teeth, and kill the armed men that grow from them. Jason accepts the challenge, while the Argonauts regard it as nearly impossible.

l: Chalciope, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Chalciope, daughter of Aeetes and sister of Medea, rejoices when her sons return and embraces them. She later withdraws to her chamber to avoid Aeetes’ anger.

l: Argus, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Argus explains to Aeetes why the sons of Phrixus and the Argonauts have come, presenting Jason as a kinsman and offering service against the Sauromatae. After Aeetes sets the challenge, Argus advises Jason to seek the aid of his mother and Medea, who knows magic taught by Hecate.

l: Hera, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Hera spreads a thick mist over the city so that Jason and his companions can approach Aeetes’ palace unseen. She later disperses the mist when they reach the palace.

l: Eros, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Eros enters unseen through the mist, strings his bow, and shoots Medea with an arrow. His arrow causes love to burn secretly in her heart for Jason.

l: Phrixus, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Phrixus is remembered as the fugitive whom Aeetes once welcomed after he escaped his stepmother’s wiles and a sacrifice prepared by his father. His sons return to Aea seeking Orchomenus and are used by Argus to explain the expedition’s connection to the golden fleece.

l: sons of Phrixus, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: The sons of Phrixus accompany Jason to Aeetes’ palace and explain that they reached the island of Enyalius after their ship was destroyed. Argus speaks for them, saying that they and the Argonauts came to seek the return of the fleece to Hellas.

l: Hecate, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Hecate has taught Medea to handle magic herbs gathered from the land and flowing waters. Her instruction makes Medea a possible source of aid against the bronze-footed bulls and the other dangers of Aeetes’ contest.

l: Hellas, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Hellas is the homeland to which the golden fleece is supposed to return. Jason also promises that, if Aeetes grants his request, all Hellas will proclaim the king’s fame.

l: Colchis, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Colchis is Aeetes’ land, where the Argonauts arrive and where the golden fleece is kept. The text also describes Colchian customs, including suspending dead men from trees rather than burning or burying them.

l: Aea, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Aea is the city and region ruled by Aeetes, which Jason and his companions reach under Hera’s protection. The sons of Phrixus and the Argonauts come there seeking the golden fleece.

l: palace of Aeetes, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: The palace of Aeetes has imposing gates, columns, inner courts, chambers, galleries, and wondrous fountains made by Hephaestus. Jason’s delegation enters it, shares a meal, and hears Aeetes announce the contest.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: The ship of the Argonauts is described as having been fashioned by Pallas Athena and as stronger than the ships of the Colchians. It can move swiftly before the wind or under the rowers’ labor and remains intact despite violent winds.

l: the fire-breathing bronze bulls, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Aeetes possesses two bulls with bronze feet that breathe fire from their mouths and pasture on the plain of Ares. He requires Jason to yoke and drive them as the first part of the contest.

l: the dragon’s teeth, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Aeetes gives Jason the task of casting serpent’s teeth into the furrows after ploughing the field of Ares. The teeth are described as seed that produces armed men.

l: earthborn armed men, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: The serpent’s teeth grow into earthborn men armed in bronze. Jason is required to kill them with his spear on the same day that he ploughs the field.

l: magic herbs, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Medea knows magic herbs that Hecate taught her to use. These herbs can quench unwearied fire and can even halt rushing rivers, the stars, and the paths of the moon.

l: Love, The Argonautica, Now the heroes apart in ambush, in a back-water of the river, were met
s: Love enters Medea’s heart when Eros shoots her, leaving her distracted, fearful, and unable to stop thinking about Jason. It causes her to pity Jason’s danger and to consider his survival as though it were her own concern.

l: The Argonautica, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: The gods send a sign when a dove fleeing a hawk falls into Jason’s lap and the hawk is impaled on the ship’s stern-ornament. Mopsus interprets the sign as a command to seek the maiden with the aid of the Cyprian goddess and to follow Argus’s counsel. Idas objects to relying on women, doves, hawks, and supplication instead of warfare, but Jason orders Argus to go to the city and directs the Argonauts to bring the ship openly to shore.

l: the sign, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: The sign consists of a trembling dove escaping a mighty hawk, falling into Jason’s lap, while the hawk falls impaled on the ship’s stern-ornament. Mopsus interprets it as showing that the Argonauts should seek the maiden with the help of the Cyprian goddess.

l: Jason, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: Jason agrees that Argus should set forth because this plan pleases the group. He orders the Argonauts to move from the river, fasten the hawsers to the shore, and stop hiding from the battle-cry.

l: Mopsus, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: Mopsus gives a prophetic interpretation of the dove and hawk. He says the Argonauts should call on Cytherea, seek out the maiden, and follow Argus’s counsel.

l: Argonauts, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: The Argonauts approve Mopsus’s interpretation while remembering Phineus’s injunctions. At Jason’s command, they draw the anchors aboard and row the ship close to shore, a little away from the back-water.

l: Medea, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: The maiden is the person whom Mopsus urges the Argonauts to seek and entreat with manifold skill. He believes she will not reject their prayer if Phineus’s prediction is true.

l: Phineus, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: Phineus is remembered as having said that the Argonauts’ return should happen with the help of the Cyprian goddess. His injunctions support Mopsus’s interpretation of the sign.

l: Aphrodite, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: Aphrodite is referred to as the Cyprian goddess, Cytherea, and Cypris. Mopsus says the dove was her gentle bird and calls on her to aid the Argonauts.

l: Argus, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: Argus’s counsel is approved by Mopsus and the Argonauts. Jason sends Argus quickly to the city after deciding that he should set forth.

l: Idas, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: Apharcian Idas angrily rejects the plan to seek help from Cypris and to rely on doves and hawks. He argues that the group should depend on the strength of Enyalius and on deeds of war instead of supplication.

l: Argo, The Argonautica, Thus he spake, and the gods in their goodwill gave them a sign. A
s: The hawk in the sign falls impaled on the ship’s stern-ornament. On Jason’s order, the Argonauts draw the ship’s anchors aboard, row it close to the shore, and fasten its hawsers there.
